rationale: B wins because it is more strategically allergic to the landmine: the unnamed supplier. Its line, "If the company will not disclose the source, do not pitch this angle," is the right comms posture before anyone starts spraying pitches. A is strong, but keeping "Patients priced out of branded weight-loss drugs now have a cheaper option" as a live angle before there is a real price or patient makes it a little too eager.
gaps_in_A: "branded drugmakers want it stopped" overstates the fact pattern. The update says manufacturers "pushed back," not that they are seeking to stop the product.
"Patients priced out of branded weight-loss drugs" is plausible, but not in the provided facts. No patient, no actual price, no proof that anyone is priced out.
"whether the model is allowed to exist" turns an FDA risk flag into an existential legal question. That may be true, but the update does not prove it.

"With at-home blood tests, telehealth moves from writing prescriptions to running diagnostics" risks making an optional lab feature sound like a care-model transformation before we know whether testing is required or clinically consequential.
gaps_in_B: "Hims & Hers won't say where its compounded semaglutide comes from" is too hot. The facts say the source is not named; they do not prove the company refused to disclose it.
"a prescription by video" invents the visit mode. The update says telehealth visit; it could be video, async questionnaire, or something else.

"ongoing FDA-versus-compounders dispute that is already being reported" imports outside context not in the update. The supplied facts establish FDA risk flags and manufacturer pushback, not a reported FDA-versus-compounders fight.

The set misses a clean consumer access/risk angle. Refusing "Patients finally have an alternative to $1,000-a-month weight-loss drugs" is right because the price is invented, but the grounded version is cheaper access with an FDA warning attached.
